title: Mechanisms of Change
subtitle: A plural account of how EMDR may help
altText: Chalkboard-style clinical neuroscience diagram illustrating mechanisms of change across threat, memory, regulation and treatment systems.
learningObjectives: Explain mechanisms of change in clinically accurate language.
Distinguish established findings from theoretical or mixed claims in mechanisms of change.
Identify one limitation or safety implication relevant to mechanisms of change.

sections.explainSimply: EMDR may work through several overlapping processes rather than one special mechanism.
sections.explainLikePsychologist: Exposure, dual attention, working-memory taxation, expectancy violation, reappraisal, therapeutic alliance and memory updating may all contribute.
sections.advancedClinicalDetail: Dismantling studies support a role for eye movements in reducing memory vividness, but comparative treatment efficacy does not establish a unique mechanism.
sections.thinkOfItLike: Think of mechanisms of change as one part of a dynamic safety-and-learning system rather than a single switch.
sections.whyPsychologistsCare: Psychologists need mechanisms of change to connect symptoms with learning, context, risk and treatment choice without reducing the person to a brain scan.
sections.clinicalPearl: Clinical pearl: use mechanisms of change to sharpen formulation, not to replace phenomenology or outcome measurement.
sections.practicalExample: A clinician uses mechanisms of change to formulate triggers, state shifts, avoidance and functional impact, then monitors whether intervention improves daily life rather than relying on presumed neural change.
sections.limitationsCautions: Avoid mechanism monoculture. Evidence classification: mixed, multi-mechanism evidence.
